description:
Here's a shorter version without emojis or bullet points:

I'm Ilyes Arfa, an engineering student from Tunisia with a passion for space. For the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, I want to build an interactive, layered map of a real Martian site. It will combine NASA imagery, elevation, mineral, and weather data to help astronauts plan safe Marswalks and do real science on the way.

I bring skills in mechanical, electrical, and embedded systems, computer vision ,
summary: Martian Map is Google Maps directions for one Marswalk. Tools like Mars Trek map Mars at global and regional scale, but astronauts need the few square kilometres of a single excursion, at walking scale. We built a planner for a 2 × 2 km site in the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp, Gale Crater. These are the formations Curiosity studied in 2025–26, and the example the challenge itself gives. The map layers NASA data at 2 m resolution: HiRISE imagery, the USGS Gale elevation model, THEMIS thermal data and CRISM minerals, plus sand and rocky ground mapped from HiRISE. For two suited astronauts and a support rover, it plans a route through Curiosity's real science stops that keeps to the ridges and avoids sand and steep ground. It gives a GO / NO-GO verdict with reasons (oxygen, point of no return, sunset, radiation, space weather, radio contact). It has three views: habitat planning, a crew tablet and a helmet HUD. Mission control can follow the crew live and re-plan the rest of the walk. Every number is labelled observed, derived or assumed.
details:
What it does

Martian Map plans and supports one surface excursion at walking scale. The crew picks science stops: Curiosity's real 2025–26 boxwork stops, any spot on the map, or both. The app then plans habitat → stops → habitat for two suited astronauts and a support rover.

  • Route: the safest route by default. It keeps to the ridges and avoids loose sand, boulders and slopes over 15°; ground at 25° or more is impassable. A faster route is offered only if it saves at least 5 minutes, with the trade-off spelled out.
    • oxygen budget, with a 30-minute reserve
    • point of no return, using a walk home 1.5× slower than planned
    • sunset, from our own Mars clock
    • radiation and space-weather alerts
    • radio line of sight to the habitat and the rover
    • time spent on sand and steep ground
  • Science stops: each stop explains what to study and why (from Curiosity's mission blog). It shows real Curiosity photos taken there and a 360° view rendered from the terrain, and says who does what (EV1, EV2, rover).
  • Crew tablet: next stop, bearing, oxygen left, live warnings, and an Abort button that routes the crew to the nearest safe haven.
    • shareable plan links and saved plans
    • a printable two-page Marswalk card
    • a voice copilot that answers what-if questions such as "can we stay 20 more minutes?"

How it works

  • Data pipeline (Python): turns NASA and USGS data into a 1000 × 1000 grid of 2 m cells over the site, holding elevation, slope and terrain type.
  • Route search: A* runs in a Web Worker. Walking speed comes from Tobler's hiking function times a spacesuit factor, and Dijkstra gives the walk-home time from every cell.
  • Mars clock: sun position and sunset use NASA's Mars24 algorithm. We checked it against Mars24's published examples and against Curiosity's REMS sunrise and sunset times.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Safety first: every verdict comes with its reasons and safety margins.
  • The right scale: the map works at the scale of one walk, which global tools don't cover.
  • Real data: the crew sees what to expect at each stop through real rover data.
  • One plan everywhere: the same plan drives the habitat, tablet and helmet views.

We hope it shows how future Mars crews could plan, carry out and re-plan a surface excursion around both safety and science.

Creativity

  • Walking scale: we used real 2 m NASA terrain and Curiosity's actual stops, so the plan is grounded in a place a rover has really walked.
  • Thermal and minerals: the night-time thermal and CRISM mineral layers are cross-checks for sand and science.
  • Real stops: every stop pairs a rover photo with a terrain view.
  • Live mission control: the walk can be re-planned around problems without changing the part already walked.

Factors we considered

  • Suit limits: reduced mobility in a suit and the oxygen limits.
  • Getting home: an emergency walk home slower than planned, and the rover as a mobile safe haven.
  • Daylight and space weather: sunset times and space-weather alerts.
  • Communications: radio shadow behind terrain.
  • Scientific honesty: each value is labelled OBSERVED, DERIVED, MODELED (our assumption) or MOCK, and nothing assumed is shown as measured.

Tools

  • Web app: TypeScript, React, Leaflet, Vite and Vitest; a static site on Vercel.
  • Data pipeline: Python, NumPy, rasterio/GDAL and pytest.
  • Voice copilot (optional): FastAPI, Ollama with Qwen3 8B, and faster-whisper.

All are open source. Source code: https://github.com/MakkiAloulou/Interplanetary-Survival-Guide-Martian-Map
